title: Breaking And Entering: Pulling Back The Curtain On YEARN IV
summary: One half of the duo behind Triple R’s Album of the Week in May of 2025, Kuya Neil, dropped into the studio on the release week of his and Teether’s collaborative album, YEARN IV. Kuya Neil talks about the behind the scenes of writing the album and its contrast in recording from the duo’s two previously released mixtapes. While the two performing producers have always drawn influence from genres like electronica and metal, Kuya Neil talks about how this time they went down to the Mornington Peninsula to intentionally slow down and refine their sound.
transcript:
Kuya Neil joined Lauren Taylor and Simon Winkler in the Triple R studios in the release week of YEARN IV, his album with Teether. Broadcast on Breaking and Entering, Triple R, 8 May 2025.

Simon: Been loving the chance, both Lauren and I, to dive deeper into the record after having been playing all the singles, and really enjoying, of course, the fusion of hip-hop, electronic, metal, punk, club music styles. As always, we were talking a little bit before the break about your history as a producer, and just the evolution through all these local, hyper-specific sounds as well as some really international influences, which I guess we'd love to talk to you a bit more about.

The album itself is not only musically expansive, but I suppose thematically looks at issues like alienation, internet-era nostalgia and the search for meaning. So some big questions that you and Teether are exploring. But the way in which it was made is also kind of fascinating for us as well. You've made two mixtapes previously, GLYPH and STRESSOR. There was the EP that was your, I guess, initial foray. But this one, you rented a Mornington Peninsula [Unclear audio at 00:01:18–00:01:22]. Is that right? And just kind of dug in?

Neil: Yeah. We were in a house for like a week in Rye, Mornington Peninsula, where all we did was just make music every day, go to the beach, cook food.

Host: You've talked about it being like you were teenagers, jamming in your bedrooms.

Neil: Yeah, it's like their parents were away or something. Yeah, it was really nice.

Host: Because you're from down that way, aren't you?

Neil: Yeah, I'm from Hastings. I don't know if people know where Hastings is, but it's, I guess, maybe a little bit further down from Frankston, if anyone knows where Frankston is. So it was cool to go back. It was very scenic and slower pace. I think that's what we really needed during that time, because the year before we had released STRESSOR, and we were, I guess, just playing shows all the time. So this was a break for us to just get away and focus on music again. So it was cool.

Host: And I guess you make music in all kinds of different ways, sharing files over the internet, but perhaps this was a really important way of connecting emotionally and physically.

Neil: Yeah, because we were just there together, and we were playing everything together. So the process had definitely become more collaborative over the year. [Unclear audio at 00:02:29–00:02:31] During that week, we were both playing guitar, playing keyboards. It felt more like a band jamming and making songs together that way, as opposed to previously, where I would be making the beat and Teether would be writing. It would be quite a separated process. So it felt very together and very hands-on.

Host: Were there unexpected moments that emerged from the jam sessions and recording?

Neil: Yeah, absolutely. I think a lot of the rock influences came through playing guitar and bass, and I think having a lot more fun as well, being more silly and playful because we had that time. We didn't have this pressure on us, which I think we felt a lot the previous year: we'd have two hours after work or before work where we're like, 'We have to make a song,' and we're very focused on completing music. So I think to have this time where we can just play around and let ideas sit and not rush it was really, really important.

Host: We're talking about guitars. Of course, you're both fascinated and experienced in playing guitar-based music. Teether has talked a lot about his background in metal, and we played just before a track from Cocteau Twins, who I think is a band that was pretty important for you. Is that right?

Neil: Yeah, for sure. Well, I've been listening to a lot of Cocteau Twins recently. I think just the guitar tone I really love a lot, and I try to emulate that a bit with the live show.

Host: And what about with metal? Was that something that was big for you as a kid?

Neil: I did. My cousin Rex from the Philippines, he was someone who taught me the guitar when I was younger, and he was a huge metalhead, and nu metal was really big at the time, like Linkin Park and Papa Roach, bands like that. [Unclear audio at 00:04:10–00:04:12] And, yeah, playing metal songs as a teenager was a way that I got better at the instrument. I wasn't necessarily only into that music. I liked a lot of other stuff, but that was probably the most fun to play at home.

Host: It's highly technical.

Neil: Yeah, absolutely. It's the most nerdy kind of one, where musicianship is super important. I think a lot of other genres that I liked, it wasn't very fashionable to be good at an instrument, like punk bands. It was cool to not know how to play, whereas in metal and stuff, it was all about chops.

Host: I was reading that you and Teether apparently have a shared love, or you're bonding over your shared love, of Metallica. Is that right?

Neil: Yeah, we both love Metallica. Teether's probably the bigger Metallica fan than me, but we both listened to a lot of that growing up, and I had all the Metallica DVDs, burnt ones from the Philippines, bootlegs and stuff.

Host: I suppose if we're talking about nostalgia and your upbringing, something else that you have both cited is the importance of early internet culture on this record, I suppose the project more generally. You have stated this idea of being raised by the internet, and musically trying to explore that soundscape. Could you describe a little bit about what that means to you, the early internet, and how it sounds?

Neil: Yeah, I think lower quality MP3, pre-streaming sort of sound, using software like LimeWire or Kazaa, even early Napster; my sister showed me that stuff early on. I think it's the process of digging for stuff online in a time where it was a lot more free, or wild, wild west internet.

Host: The promise of the early internet.

Neil: Yeah, absolutely. It was quite utopian anyways. People could customise their own pages; people had a sense of not only anonymity, but autonomy over what they're presenting. There was a lot more of that.

Host: Are we talking MySpace pages?

Neil: Yeah, absolutely. Even before MySpace, people would make their own websites. Learning how to code was kind of a thing that young people were doing, and experimenting with that as a creative thing. And obviously now it's a lot different, but I miss that era a lot.

Host: And I think just creating your own little universe, because I suppose identity really forms a core part of this new album as well.

Neil: Yeah, for sure, for sure.

[Unclear audio at 00:06:28–00:06:30]

Simon: And I guess, as well, bridging past and present, your new record brings together, as I mentioned earlier, hyper-local and global influences. What elements of the Naarm/Melbourne music community and its sound are you including?

[Unclear audio at 00:06:44–00:06:46]

Neil: I think so many. Maybe for Teether it would be a lot of the underground rap stuff, particularly stuff that's coming out of the southeast, artists like Chef Chung and producers like Hawkrada, who are making more lo-fi, abstract hip-hop. And for myself, it would definitely be the club scene. So the DJs who are playing at Miscellania and stuff like that: people playing jungle, people playing ballroom, vogue music, Jersey club, all electronic dance music, I think.

Host: The album itself features a bunch of collaborators too, like Nerdie from 1300, Alice Skye and Stoneset as well. Can you tell us more about their involvement?

Neil: Yeah. Stoneset actually came to the recording session and hung out with us for a few days, and we just were sharing songs that we were working on, and then the 'DIAL UP' beat: immediately when I heard that, I was like, 'Oh, this is amazing.' And then I just jumped on it quickly and added a couple of flourishes, and then Teether was in the bathroom or something, and when [Unclear audio at 00:07:50–00:07:53] walked out, we'd already finished the song. So he was like, 'Oh, let's record this.' So it was one of those really immediate kind of things where we just fell in love with the sound, and he's such an incredible producer.

[Unclear audio at 00:07:59–00:08:02] Alice, it was a bit different. We made the song during the writing trip, but during that time, I kept thinking of Natalie Imbruglia's 'Torn' music video. That kept playing in my mind when I was making that track, and I was like, 'Oh, this feels like Australiana,' like that kind of watching videos on Rage or something.

Host: Was that a big ritual for you growing up?

Neil: Yeah, absolutely. Rage was a big part. That's how I would get put onto a lot of stuff, through music videos. So Alice just felt like the perfect person for that. We were already friends, and we just reached out to her, and she was into the track, and went to her place and just recorded it. [Unclear audio at 00:08:38–00:08:41] And who's the other person?

Host: Oh, 1300, Nerdie from 1300.

Neil: Yeah, that was the first time we ever hung out. We just got some lunch together. He started playing the guitar. He was just mucking around. He wasn't really playing anything seriously, but I was recording everything. And then I just used the guitar parts that he made, and I produced a track with that. He probably doesn't even really remember it. I've spoken to him about it. He's like, 'What song is that?' So I don't think it even really registered in his mind, but I really liked it.

Host: He was deep in the flow state while he made that one.

Neil: Yeah, probably.

[Unclear audio at 00:09:09–00:09:12]

Host: Well, speaking of flow, there's a real ebb and flow with the energy of the record as well. You have released, as we mentioned, a couple of mixtapes, but this one is officially your, I guess, your debut full-length release, because you've talked about it really being a cohesive narrative and musical statement. Could you tell us a little bit about the sequencing of this album and the story that it's telling?

[Unclear audio at 00:09:33–00:09:35]

Neil: Yeah, I think, with the sequencing, honestly, I have to give that to Ben O'Connor from Chapter Music. He's really good at sequencing records. He loves to do it, and I kind of trusted him with that. I had a rough sequence that is more maybe around the order in which things are made, but that doesn't always make sense for the listeners.

So I think, I usually feel like we start our records with a kind of more of a driving mission statement kind of song that's quite heavy. That's usually how we start, and then we just try to throw the listener around. So you'll probably notice that there's a lot of shifts in mood. It doesn't really ride a certain feeling consistently. It kind of just jumps around, and I think that just reflects how we consume stuff now.

Everything is pretty jarring. You can be watching on your phone, you can be scrolling through some of the most intense things ever, and then the stupidest things right straight after, so.

Host: And Neil, what are some of the core ideas that you and Teether were kind of keen to communicate on the new record?

[Unclear audio at 00:10:53–00:10:56]

Neil: I think we really just want to create something that's honest and represents where we're from and where we grew up, an honest representation of that, the reality of that, and how that kind of isolation or even boredom is what creates the imagination for music, I think.

Especially being geographically so far away from a lot of the stuff that we're inspired by, I think you can feel quite placeless being here. So I think that's sort of what we wanted to speak on: just the experience of growing up in this country and the things that are hard about that, but the things that also feed your imagination and make it really special.

[Unclear audio at 00:11:35–00:11:38]

Host: And I guess this new record, as I mentioned, out via Chapter Music, it's also one of the final releases on Chapter Music in its current form. Can you tell us a bit more about your relationship with that label, and how did you first connect with them?

Neil: It was actually through Triple R, I feel like. Paul Gorrie played some of our tracks from God of Surprises, which is our first ever release, through X Amount Records. Shout out to them. And then they just contacted us directly. So we didn't really have a relationship before that. So it's kind of like meeting for the very first time and then working together for the very first time. [Unclear audio at 00:12:13–00:12:15] But they've been really amazing, honestly. They've been super helpful, and they give us so much freedom to express what we want to express, but also give us a lot of good advice, and kind of helped us to take it more seriously.

I think we definitely come from a bit of a culture of not wanting to take things super seriously, not wanting to have ambition or not wanting to be maybe career-focused. There's maybe a bit of shame around that aspect. But I think they made that seem possible without having to compromise on the music side. So, yeah, they've just been amazing. Really friendly, helpful.

They're big fans, and they've been doing it for so long as well. So I feel like they're just good people to have around, because they're in for the long haul, you know?

Host: There's such a powerful and strong alignment with what you're all doing as well, creating communities, celebrating the artistry of others and really uplifting, which is really beautiful. And, of course, there is going to be very much a celebration of that legacy at Day Tripper. [Unclear audio at 00:13:18–00:13:20] It's going to be an incredible live experience. And I guess in the live arena, it's been a big year for you as well. I think the last time you were on Triple R might have been with Samira on The Score. I think that was ahead of Golden Plains. Is that right?

Neil: Yeah, that's right. It was, yeah, we had one show at the Gasometer.

Host: And the Golden Plains set.

Neil: Yeah, that was amazing. It was like, I don't know, such a perfect week for us. I hadn't seen [Unclear audio at 00:13:42–00:13:45], obviously, since he'd moved. So it was…

Host: The real reunion.

Neil: Yeah, reunion. But it felt like nothing had changed. I picked him up when he was in Footscray. It felt like he'd just gone to Sydney or something, or it felt like he had just gone down, you know? It didn't feel weird at all. And that week was just full of seeing friends, playing shows. It was amazing.

Host: We've lined up a song from the record to play to conclude the conversation. What can you tell us about this one?

Neil: Oh, which one is this?

Host: Oh, 'WAY OUT'.

Neil: Oh, 'WAY OUT'. Yeah, this one… I think this one, it does capture the feeling of the trip. This one is a kind of underwater feeling. We spend a lot of time at the beach, just staring at the ocean, you know, single teardrop, getting sentimental. So this is definitely capturing that.

I think it's a good middle point of the record. It has a lot of footwork and dance music elements, but also it has a kind of more nostalgic and gentle synth-y sort of line, and feels kind of organic, too. So, yeah, I think it's a good record that captures both sides.
aliases: Pulling Back The Curtain On YEARN IV
